bib.title: DeepDive: Advancing Deep Search Agents with Knowledge Graphs and Multi-Turn RL

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "DeepDive: Advancing Deep Search Agents with Knowledge Graphs and Multi-Turn RL", Rui Lu, Zhenyu Hou, Zihan Wang (equal contribution) et al., Tsinghua University / Z.AI / Northeastern. arXiv:2509.10446v2 (14 Oct 2025). Venue: "Preprint. Under review." (no conference venue printed). Year 2025.

COVERAGE: 57,416 of 57,416 chars read, all 16 pages (main text pp1-12, references 12-15, Appendix A and B pp15-16). Extraction was clean. Figures were not rendered; I only have their extracted text. Figure 8 bar values below are unlabeled in extraction order, so I do not report them.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- The 15.3% is the right headline number: DeepDive-32B (QwQ-32B backbone, SFT then RL, KG data only), full BrowseComp, first row of the paper's results.
  number: 15.3%
  setup: QwQ-32B, 32B params; KG-synthesized data; full BrowseComp (1,266 instances), turn limit raised to 128; every dataset evaluated twice and averaged; Llama-3.1-70B as judge.
  quote: "Built on this, DeepDive-32B reaches an accuracy of 15.3% on BrowseComp, surpassing many open agents—WebSailor, Search-o1, and DeepSeek-R1-Browse"
  where: p3 (Intro); Table 1, p8
- Redundancy penalty is real. It is in the abstract, in Section 2.2 (Eq. 7-9), and in an ablation. Jaccard similarity of keyword sets between all query pairs in a trajectory, averaged, then subtracted from the binary reward. Lambda = 0.1.
  number: lambda = 0.1
  setup: S(T) is the mean pairwise Jaccard over search queries in one trajectory, in [0,1]. Only the final reward is changed; it is trajectory-level, not per-query.
  quote: "r′(T) =r(T)−λ·S(T)(9) where λ <1 controls how much we reward diverse queries." and "We set the redundancy penalty coefficient to λ= 0.1."
  where: p6 (Eq. 9), p7 (training details)
- Base reward is strict binary: +1 only if every step is correctly formatted AND an LLM judge matches the final answer to ground truth; otherwise 0.
  number: none
  quote: "A trajectory T receives a +1 reward only when every step is correctly formatted, including the reason ci and the action ai, and the final answer aeos matches the ground-truth a∗."
  where: p6
- Redundancy penalty ablation (BrowseComp-266 subset).
  number: ~14% fewer tool calls; accuracy "about 20%" higher later in training. This is relative, not absolute: the plot axis is about 8-13% accuracy.
  setup: same RL settings, evaluated every 40 steps from 40 to 240; Fig 7b is accuracy and Fig 7c is tool-call counts.
  quote: "adding the redundancy penalty increases accuracy in the later training phase (about 20%) and reduces tool call counts by roughly 14% under the same conditions."
  where: p9
- Format-reward ablation.
  number: curve near 8.0 without it; about 2 points higher with it
  quote: "removing the format reward yields a curve that stays near 8.0 with almost no improvement, while adding the format reward produces a steady upward trend that remains about 2 absolute points higher throughout training."
  where: p9
- Table 1 baselines on BrowseComp (BC), with columns BC / BC-ZH / Xbench-DeepSearch / SEAL-0. Reasoning/browse flags are as printed.
  quote rows: "WebSailor-32B✓ ✓10.5 * 25.5 *53.3* -" ; "Search-o1-32B✓ ✓2.8* 17.9* 25.0* -" ; "Claude-4-Sonnet-Thinking✓ ✓14.7 30.8 53.0 37.8" ; "DeepResearch✓ ✓51.5* 42.9* - -" ; "QwQ-32B✓ ✓1.3 14.5 27.0 4.5" ; "DeepSeek-R1-0528✓ ✗3.2 28.7 37.0 5.4" ; "WebSailor-7B✓ ✓6.7* 14.2* 34.3* -" ; "ASearcher-Web-32B✓ ✓5.2* 15.6* 42.1* -" ; "WebDancer-32B✓ ✓3.8* 18.0* 39.0* -" ; "GLM-4.5-355B✓ ✓26.4 37.5 68.0 36.0" ; "GLM-4.5-Air-106B✓ ✓21.3 36.3 65.0 30.6"
  where: Table 1, p8. An asterisk means a score copied from the original paper; the rest were run by the authors.
  Note: the text says "ranks just behind OpenAI's DeepResearch and far ahead of other open-source models or agents", but Table 1 shows Claude-4-Sonnet-Thinking with browsing at 14.7, which is close to 15.3. GLM-4.5 (21.3 and 26.4) is also above it; the paper treats GLM-4.5 as downstream of DeepDive data.
  Text quote: "While most open-source models score under 10% on BrowseComp, DeepDive-32B achieved 15.3%."
- DeepDive model variants from Table 1 (BC / BC-ZH / Xbench / SEAL-0).
  quote: "DeepDive-9B (sft-only) ✓ ✓ 5.6 15.7 35.0 15.2" ; "DeepDive-9B ✓ ✓ 6.3 15.1 38.0 12.2" ; "DeepDive-32B (sft-only) ✓ ✓ 9.5 23.0 48.5 23.9" ; "DeepDive-32B ✓ ✓ 15.3 29.7 51.8 25.5"
  Detail: the 9B model (GLM-Z1-9B-0414) gains little from RL. The authors say "these gains are less pronounced for the smaller 9B model, potentially because of its limited reasoning capacity or a tendency to overfit on synthetic data". The SFT-only 32B gets "9.5% on BrowseComp". Xbench for DeepDive-32B is 51.8 in Table 1 but 50.0 in Tables 2 and 3, an internal inconsistency.
  where: p7-8
- Data synthesis from KGs.
  number: 3,250 QA pairs, split 1,016 SFT and 2,234 RL
  setup: KGs are KILT and AMiner; random walk with k in [5,9], d=3, dmin=4, dmax=8 (out-degree filter on nodes); the next node is chosen by an LLM; attributes along the path are blurred (e.g. dates turned into ranges); Gemini-2.5-Pro obscures entities and writes the question; the answer is an attribute of the terminal node. Difficulty filter: GPT-4o with basic search tries each question 4 times, and the question is kept only if all 4 fail. Cold-start SFT traces: 858, from Claude-4-Sonnet-Thinking with rejection sampling.
  quote: "This process yields 3,250 deep search QA pairs, which are randomly split into 1,016 samples for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and 2,234 for Reinforcement Learning (RL)." and "Each question is tested four times—if the model solves it in any attempt, the question is discarded."
  where: p5, p6
  Caution: the intro says "3,090 high-quality deep search QAs", but the method section says 3,250. The paper is inconsistent.
- Training setup.
  number: GRPO, KL beta=0, lr 1e-6, rollout 16 samples per prompt (extraction reads "rollout size of 8, 16 samples per prompt"), batch 128, temperature 1.0, max context 51,200 during RL
  setup: Slime framework; Serper search API (top-10); Jina for click/open; actions are search, click, open (ReAct loop). SFT: 3 epochs, batch 32, lr 1e-5, context 104,800.
  quote: "To promote exploration, we set the KL penalty coefficient toβ= 0" and "The training configuration includes a rollout size of 8, 16 samples per prompt, a global batch size of 128, a temperature of 1.0, and a maximum context length of 51,200 tokens."
  where: p7
- Data ablation (Table 2, QwQ-32B backbone, BC-266 subset).
  number: BC-266 accuracy 1.9 (base), 4.9 (SFT+HotpotQA), 7.5 (SFT+KG data); RL on top: 9.2 (HotpotQA) vs 12.0 (KG data). Average tool calls (#Turn) on BC-266: 1.5, 20.2, 32.7, 33.2, 36.3.
  quote: "DeepDive-32B (SFT only) + HotpotQA 9.2 33.2 22.7 23.3 47.0 15.1 21.6 13.6+our data 12.0 36.3 29.7 24.9 50.0 16.7 25.5 14.5"
  where: Table 2, p10
- Extra side study with semi-automated i.i.d. data (human annotators plus o3 with search): 2,997 English and 275 Chinese QA pairs. The full-BrowseComp result there is 22.2% in Table 3. Section 4 prose says 20.8%, so there is an inconsistency.
  number: 22.2% (Table 3) vs "20.8%" (text)
  quote: "DeepDive-32B i.i.d data 22.2 33.9 56.0 23.0" and "the DeepDive-32B-RL model achieves an accuracy of 20.8% on the full BrowseComp benchmark, representing a 40% improvement over the previous best score of 15.3%". Table 3 also lists "DeepDive-32B (sft-only) i.i.d data 11.4 26.6 47.5 22.5". The intro says "can further lift the accuracy of the 32B-parameter model to22.2%".
  where: p10-11, p3
  Note: 15.3% is the KG-only result. Do not mix it with the 22.2% i.i.d. result.
- Test-time scaling (parallel sampling on BC-266, 8 samples).
  number: 12.0 base; majority vote 18.8; fewest-tool-calls selection 24.8; pass@8 37.6
  quote: "majority voting ... improves DeepDive-32B performance on BrowseComp-266 from 12.0 to 18.8." and "selecting the answer with the fewest tool calls, which achieves a substantial improvement from 12.0 to 24.8, approaching the theoretical upper bound of 37.6 (pass@8)."
  where: p9 (Fig 6c)
  Tool-call budget scaling: accuracy rises steadily with budget (8 to 128 calls); RL beats SFT-only at 16 or more calls.
- Generalization to easier benchmarks (Appendix A). DeepDive-32B and the SFT-only variant beat all baselines on HotpotQA (512 random questions), Frames and WebWalker. Exact bar values are not recoverable from the extraction.
  quote: "Figure 8 shows that both DeepDive-32B (SFT-only) and DeepDive-32B outperform all baselines, with reinforcement learning providing additional improvements across all benchmarks."
  where: p16
- Contamination check on BrowseComp: more than 97% of samples are Clean and none are Dirty (LLaMA-2 protocol, 10-token n-grams).
  quote: "more than 97% of the samples in the dataset are classified as Clean, and there are no samples in the Dirty category."
  where: p11
- Case study (Appendix B): search-operator use shifts during RL. Quote usage goes from about 30% to 40%, then falls below 25%; minus usage rises from 14% to 18%; OR usage goes from about 2% to 8% (the prose is self-contradictory on OR, also saying it stays between 0.8% and 1%).
  where: p16

LIMITS
- Authors' own: synthetic data difficulty is "significantly lower than datasets like BrowseComp", so performance stays far below o3 with browsing (OpenAI DeepResearch 51.5). The RL approach leads to "over-search" in DeepDive-32B. Optimal training steps and better reward design are left to future work. The 9B model gains little from RL.
- Evaluation is on a 266-question subset (BrowseComp-266) for all ablations, so those numbers are noisy. Final numbers average only two runs. Baselines mix self-run results and copied (*) results, so they are not like for like. The judge is Llama-3.1-70B.
- The redundancy-penalty accuracy gain is a small-subset curve (about 1 point on an 8-13% scale) with no seeds or error bars. Its tool-call reduction is the more solid effect.
- The paper does not state whether the penalty is part of the 15.3% run, but the method section says it is part of the reward and lambda=0.1 is given in the main training setup, so it is probably included.
- Internal inconsistencies: 3,090 vs 3,250 QA pairs; 22.2% vs 20.8%; Xbench 51.8 vs 50.0 for the same model.
- Preprint, under review; check whether a later version changed numbers.

BUILDS ON: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023); BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025); DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025); WebSailor (Li et al., 2025a); Search-o1 (Li et al., 2025b); WebThinker (Li et al., 2025c); LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al., 2023); self-consistency/majority vote (Wang et al., 2022); KL=0 for exploration (Vassoyan et al., 2025); Jaccard (Real and Vargas, 1996); contamination protocol (Touvron et al., 2023, LLaMA 2); Slime framework (Zhu et al., 2025); related to R1-Searcher, ReSearch, DeepResearcher, WebDancer, ASearcher.

CODE: no code in the paper; repo is https://github.com/THUDM/DeepDive. Formulas worth keeping (p5-6): "S(T) = 1/(T(T−1)) Σ_{i≠j} sim(qi, qj)", "sim(qi, qj) = |qi ∩ qj| / |qi ∪ qj|", "r′(T) = r(T) − λ·S(T)".

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p1): left, redundancy penalty reduces tool-call counts during RL; middle, tool-call budget vs BrowseComp success; right, RL gain over SFT on the four benchmarks (+5.8, +6.7, +1.6, +3.3 points).
- Fig 3 (p4): KG random-walk, attribute-blur, LLM-obscure pipeline diagram.
- Fig 4 (p5): RL reward diagram showing the Jaccard-based redundancy penalty, format reward and LLM judge.
- Fig 7 (p9): reward ablations.
- Fig 6c (p9): voting vs fewest-tool-calls selection.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction of figures/tables is partly scrambled, but table rows are readable. For the note at line ~403, "Knowledge-graph questions and multi-turn RL with a penalty on redundant queries. 15.3% on BrowseComp" is accurate for DeepDive-32B (QwQ-32B, KG data only, full BrowseComp). I did not read the note itself.
